Thirdly, there is an opportunity here. There is a lot of change happening, whether it be policy or new bodies like the Regulatory Innovation Office. How do we harmonise all the things that are happening in our ecosystem across the PRA, the FCA and the CMA? There is so much to contend with, and for time-poor entrepreneurs and perhaps investors with limited sized teams it is very difficult to navigate.
Does it have to be an exit? Is there scope for large companies to be supportive in all sorts of ways and help smaller businesses grow?

There is probably room for both. Some companies, if they are not bought for the tech or the talent, will need to wind up. That is a large part of any innovation economy. It is not a bad thing. It is a high-risk, high-reward business. There is also an opportunity for further partnerships, hopefully domestically, as well as international partners coming in, as Alex alluded to.
Thank you. Mr Wise.

It is an important question. Our business model requires exits. We have to return the capital at some point to our investors . T hat can come through public listings or through M&A ; we have had experiences of both and I have been through both processes. M&A is an important way of recycling capital into the ecosystem and releasing some of that talent back into the ecosystem. I am sure Alex can talk to you at length about the many people at DeepMind who may now work at Wayve post the Google acquisition. If Google had not made that acquisition, it is unclear whether DeepMind would have been able to have access to the resources it needed to build that talent base. So there is an important flywheel effect here.
We hear that all the talent that is grown by DeepMind then goes to the States.

I speak to lots of DeepMind teams who are looking at more entrepreneurial endeavours at the moment , and we have invested in some of them. Not all of them have left these shores , I can promise you that much. It is a good example, because I believe Cadbury was taken over in the same week as DeepMind was. I was on the radio talking about DeepMind and the person opposite me was talking about Cadbury, and there was a lot more public scrutiny at the time of the Cadbury takeover than the DeepMind one. The CMA’s role is not an easy one. It has been on a journey over the last five years. Right now, at least in my experience, the CMA is more communicative than it has ever been, which is really important , and at the moment is getting praise compared to its US peer.

The one thing I would stress, though, is that when you talk about scale-up , some of that scale is achieved inorganically. The CMA is just as harsh, if not harsher, at looking at internal roll-ups—British companies buying other British companies to scale—as it is in international takeovers, where there is just no path for many companies to get to a competitive level with their international peers if they cannot also take over other British companies. Making sure that we are not forcing British companies to stay small by not allowing them to grow through blocking small takeovers is important.
What is your average holding time until you exit?
Seven years is our average. We hope that it is longer than that, because if it is longer than that it has generally gone better.

Q11 Can we talk now about the role of hubs, incubators and other ways of supporting scale-ups? There are two questions I would love to hear you all on. First, how important are place-based schemes, clusters and hubs? Do they deliver something that you cannot get elsewhere. The second thing is the role of universities in helping start-ups and then scale-ups.

Mr Holmes, can we start with you, because you have had very direct experience working in White City with Imperial? There is a similar thing happening in Manchester. Could you help us by telling us what you think has worked well, what we might be able to learn from elsewhere , and where there are things that you think did not go quite as well?

My direct experience is partnering with Imperial in the White City Innovation District. If we describe what we have as an innovation cluster and define what that means for this group, it brings together a combination of businesses of course, and, importantly, access to talent, access to mentorship and the networks that any scaling business needs in order to scale. It is not just about the great idea and the capital; you need the support system. Covid had its couple of years of people working remotely, but we had a rapid return to the office in west London following the pandemic, which is important.

The question made reference to a place-based scheme. We see that day to day with the networking events, the learning and development, the fact that young people want to be in the office because they know they will learn more from each other, meet their mentors and bump into their neighbours who are in a similar industry sector. The value of a cluster is that it helps in some sense to de-risk the decisions from a business perspective. If you are a talented individual going to join a company and you are in a cluster, that is lower risk than moving somewhere where there is only one company.
The second part of the question was about the role of the universities.

Yes. I am interested in how clusters form and whether there are things we should be urging to get clusters to form , or whether these happen naturally in the world of universities in helping them to come together.

To give some context, Scale Space came into being through a number of years of discussion between the local council of Hammersmith and Fulham, Imperial College London and Blenheim Chalcot , which at the time was based in Hammersmith but had run out of space at that location. It took several years of discussion and the opportunity on Imperial’s White City campus, which it acquired during the financial crisis. A combination of factors resulted in a fairly unique joint venture partnership, and the opportunity arose to deploy that. It would not have been possible without Imperial’s land , resources and support. Imperial is leading the way on this being a successful cluster.

Clearly, there is a large number of high-quality university institutions, some of which are going through a period of stress, but Imperial is perhaps shining a light on what can be done. There are other successful examples and university partnerships with various degrees of success. The university angle is interesting and important , because that is one area where the UK has a competitive advantage in the number of world-leading institutions. However, that is not translating into the number of billion-dollar scale-ups coming through the system. So the more that universities can be encouraged to partner with business and to form these clusters , the better. Hopefully, west London is a good example of what can be replicated elsewhere in the UK.
There is an example in west London White City, but what do we need to be urging universities and others to do? What is the policy that we need to be promoting?

One consideration is the way that grant funding is structured. There are a number of grants that encourage or stipulate joint academic and business input. At the moment , there are two fairly discrete pools that could be better connected. When you compare the culture of UK institutions or universities as opposed to the US, in the UK we have world-leading research institutions but with less of a focus on translating those into commercially successful businesses, which is more of a focus in the US. That can perhaps be stimulated through reviewing the way the grant funding is structured and particularly encouraging more partnerships between universities and businesses.

Thank you. I wonder whether any of our other guests today have views about the role of universities and where we should be looking for more reform to deliver the sorts of things that we are trying to deliver.

Can I make a quick comment on grant funding? In our experience, grant funding through Innovate UK—I looked it up the other day—costs the taxpayer £900 million a year. This is severely broken and something that could be looked at. In our experience, often the results of where this money is allocated are largely random, not well formulated on the venture capital-style approach or on viability of business. Often, they go to projects that are more political than will actually produce leading outcomes that will really move the needle for the country. I want to separate this from the academic grants. I cannot comment on that area.

When it comes to the company grant process, our experience going through those processes was certainly not positive. There was a lot of time spent and a lot of money flowing through to the grant writer businesses , but very little value come out from ours or other businesses that I have seen go through those processes. That is on grants.

On universities, there are two types of companies that can come out of universities. One is companies that draw on IP that has been developed through the university. Wayve was not that, but my observation of those companies is that they often get stuck in tech transfer processes , and a lot of innovation is killed or slowed down by some of th o se processes.

My experience at Cambridge University has some positive aspects, but in general I have read and seen reports and had friends and entrepreneurs who have gone through those experiences where the university takes a high equity ownership and has very slow processes or a lot of IP grab that will prevent those companies being launched into a venture scale-up model. That could certainly be vastly improved for the benefit of the deep tech sector in the UK. For companies that do not take IP out of universities, again it is more of a talent hub. My experience was meeting friends and co-founders at the universities, and they can be a great source of that.
Thank you. Erin.

B uilding on Alex’s comments, I very much welcome the recent university spin-out review. A lot of the findings in there are very relevant with respect to time to spin out, especially on tech transfer, and capping the ownership that universities can take. Unfortunately, we have been talking about this for at least the 17 years that I have been here. It really is about implementation and co-ordination and harmonising our amazing universities to set these businesses up for success more quickly.

The role of clusters post spin-out becomes very important. A lot of what we have observed at least is that some of the spin-outs that are IP-led—healthcare, life sciences and deep tech-related—can perhaps use additional commercialisation talent to come in and join the early-stage spin-out . Having clusters like Scale Space that Mike runs where you have a combination of deep technical expertise and folks who have commercialised technology in a different scale flattens the learning curve, and the time to market becomes quicker.

Q12 Something that came out of a conversation that some of us had in San Francisco some weeks ago with founders was the thought that in the US certainly there is much more interchange between universities and what you are doing and promoting, and that here you are either one or the other. Do you think that is an issue and something we should be thinking about?

I do, and I see Alex vigorously nodding. You see in the US — Stanford, MIT, you name it — professors going in and out, and universities spinning out and taking their ideas with them. We seem to have quite separate silos still, so that is a real opportunity for us to facilitate and incentivise.
Thank you. Alex, you were nodding.
Yes, I have nothing further to add . I agree.
Thank you .

All these comments are important. I would just like to add one more point beyond commercialisation, which is access to resources for researchers today. The university is incredibly important and still a hub of innovation, but the trend over the last decade has increasingly been that the resources around private R&D labs, in particular those owned by big technology companies, are becoming so much more powerful and influential that universities are struggling to compete.

I spoke to a University of Oxford graduate researcher last week working on a flood - plain modelling service—very important as we go through changes in the weather—and he is in a queue to access CPU compute with the Brunel infrastructure around Bristol. Were he at Google DeepMind now, he would have access to almost unlimited compute power as it builds that model , and it would look for ways to commercialise that over time. As an individual, he has to make that trade-off. Does he want to stay with the wonderful peers he has and the wonderful tutor he has at Oxford, or does he want to get paid significant sums of money and have access to all the resources he needs to build that model? Eventually, the allure of the university system will break down beyond the nice dining at high table unless we provide them with the resources to compete or at least find novel areas that those large technology companies are yet to focus on.
That is really interesting and clear. Thank you .

Q13 It is very interesting. Mr Holmes, you mentioned culture. Do you think we can encourage a much more entrepreneurial culture in UK universities as they do in Stanford and on the west coast? Is it a lack of ambition, or are we just very risk averse?

It is a combination of factors. Changing the cultural stance of a country is not an overnight job. There is something to be said about creating the incentives and conditions in which the appropriate amount of risk-taking is rewarded. The UK has an interesting relationship with risk; it is seen as a bad word and not something to be desired. However, in reality, you need to take risks to innovate and break new ground. That is definitely a factor.

However, in more practical terms, to respond to one of the previous questions, from a policy perspective, sustaining funding for schemes that support university innovation activities such as the Higher Education Innovation Fund is important. The university spin-out review referenced earlier also recommended £20 million of proof-of-concept funding, which has not yet been implemented. That would be useful if it was taken forward. Universities have to make their own decisions about how to operate. There should be recognition that we are in a really strong position today with regard to the quality of our university ecosystem. However, it is not translating through to the outcomes that we would want as a country. Anything that can be done to support the universities around entrepreneurial activities and innovation should be supported.

Q14 Thank you. Ms Platts, you mentioned the report that was looking at spin-out s . One thing it suggested was that PhD students should be sent to companies to learn some entrepreneurial techniques as well. Do you think that would be possible and that companies would be interested in trying to encourage that?

I think it is a wonderful idea. The panel’s discussion on talent being the No. 1 linchpin in this whole ecosystem coming together, to be able to cross-fertilise, establish companies with PhDs, to give the PhDs access to not just working in established companies but seeing how it feels to work in a start-up, what you can do with passion and ambition, is very welcome and something that I hope we facilitate.

That is exactly what I was fortunate enough to be able to do. I took six months out of my PhD and went to Silicon Valley and joined a series A-stage robotics company called Skydio , where I was able to continue my research with the benefit of commercial resources. I was also immersed in and learned about how to build a venture-backed company. I did not know what venture capital was before that experience. Off the back of that, it set me off on the path of being able to build Wayve to where we are today. It was a very formative experience for me.

In fact, I first met Alex while he was at university because it was so rare to find someone who was doing a PhD and had gone to San Francisco to get experience of a start-up. It was the only reason why I reached out initially.

That is interesting, because in San Francisco we were told that if you are at Stanford and doing a doctorate you immediately think of also doing a business project, but that if you did that at Cambridge or Oxford you might get sent down. Maybe that was an extreme view.

Q15 I want to go a little bit below PhDs. The climate has changed in this country. Young people may go to university , but they may take an apprenticeship. Some universities are good at delivering that; some are not very good. You also have FE colleges as part of that process.

First, d o you recognise those changes that are taking place and the part they play in delivering skills? Secondly, Alex, it was you who said, “I owe such a debt of gratitude to my mentor”. I am paraphrasing your words, but it was pretty fulsome praise. Do each of you play your part in delivering these new entrepreneurs by

I have supported an apprenticeships business for a long time based in Manchester—for the last five years , in fact. So I think it is an incredibly important opportunity. In fact, if you look at the reasons why people in the UK say they go into entrepreneurial roles at least, less than 10% say that it is because of their educational background. A vast majority of people say that it is because of role models and mentors they had around them as they grew up.

Even if you do go into further education, there is no reason why you may become more entrepreneurial and not go down that route. We are increasingly seeing both a willingness by young people to take apprenticeship routes and other types of formal training over further education , and more young people wanting to be entrepreneurs. They also have the opportunity now to get experience of that at a younger age, whether that be buying and selling things on eBay and Depop or consuming content on YouTube from other entrepreneurs. We are providing younger people with more routes to getting work experience, finding role models and starting businesses, and they have access to more content. I am fully supportive of it.

As to mentorship, we are an active venture fund. We almost always take board seats. Therefore, we take our governance and fiduciary responsibilities very seriously as well as supporting our founders. We launched something called the founders well-being programme, which tries to provide mental and physical support to founders, because entrepreneurs are very hard-working people and need that kind of support. We hope to expand that mentorship to other areas of our sector, whether it is product officers or finance officers.

Britain as a whole is not as good at this as the US. If you speak to most of my peers in Silicon Valley, if they work in product at, let us say, Facebook, their friends and peers almost always product at Google and at Snapchat. A lot of Brits’ friends are people they went to university and school with. That is wonderful, but we do not have the same cultural leaning towards creating communities of like-minded individuals who are perhaps pursuing a similar kind of skill or path. Informal networks are equally important, and there is probably more that private sector individuals like me and government have to do.

This is such an important point about bringing in more diverse talent into innovation, especially from a socioeconomic perspective. I am a good example of a non-technologist having made a career in the innovation ecosystem, starting with answering the phones 20-something years ago. There is a narrative that we are all responsible for breaking that down. You do not need a PhD to be successful in the tech industry. You do not need to have spent X amount of money on private education to be successful. That is the beauty of this ecosystem; with some luck and hard work, you can have a wonderful career. There is a fantastic opportunity in this country to crowd in, whether it be apprentice or just entry-level folks who can get on the rocket ship and enjoy the ride and hopefully make a really successful career of it.

All of us are very much responsible for mentoring. It is a great point. In our role in HSBC innovation banking, we see ourselves as a convener of the ecosystem. We have 5,000 tech companies and 350 funds. We are working with people like Sie Ventures, Alma Angels or Black Seed. Trying to funnel more resources and investment into overlooked founders from different backgrounds is a big role that we play in the ecosystem.
I am thinking of computer games, an area where young people are just phenomenal with their contribution. Alex and Michael, do you want to add anything?

I would love to do more of this in the future, but right now I am so focused and devoted to building Wayve that, unfortunately, I do not have much time to help with mentorship outside our team. Within our team, we bring on a number of different interns from universities every year, and we are rapidly growing up an engineering base. The exciting thing about where we are at the moment is that we are starting to see internal leaders grow in our company as well rather than just hiring in leaders. We have had enough time that we are starting to see the growth of some people in our company stepping up, leading teams, delivering new outcomes, and that has been great to see and amazing to work with over the last couple of years.

On the topic of mentorship , f or me this really comes back to clusters again. In our cluster in west London, there are a huge number of very valuable mentorships that form quite naturally. Mentorship means different things to different people , and around this room you would all have a slightly different definition.

On a personal note, I try, although I would say that I am not an entrepreneur. My job is to set the environment where the other CEOs and entrepreneurs will be in a position and encouraged to mentor other people in the community through putting on events and networking and different initiatives. I play a slightly different role in that aspect, but I recognise that it is hugely important and valuable for any ecosystem.
Thank you . I appreciate the response.

Q16 Lord Kamall : One of the issues we heard in San Francisco when comparing British universities to American universities and spin-out s or scale-ups was that some of the people who were British and had started over here said to us that they thought some of the British universities did not really understand the environment or were too greedy in the stake they wanted to take in the start-up company. Is that your experience, any of you, and is that our message to our universities—to try to give these spin-out s or start-ups a bit of slack to allow them to grow?

Having some framework or harmonisation of the equity stakes that universities can take for tech transfers will be exceptionally helpful. A lot of the US universities do not take anything , or it is 10% or less. I do not think the variance that we see across the board is helpful. I am an advocate of some sort of framework that perhaps caps the percentage that universities can take.
Lord Kamall : That is very helpful, thank you.

Q17 We will quickly rattle through a series of three or four questions about what else government can do apart from what we have already discussed. I want to start with government procurement and the access that scale-up companies have to government procurement. James and Erin, with your overview, do you see scale-ups being able to access government procurement contracts? Is there more government should do to open that up?

Yes, it is an ongoing challenge. The Procurement Act, which has been passed and will come into effect next year, will be a welcome change. It will lower the size of some of the contracts, which will make them more applicable to start-ups, and there will be some more pressure to look at SMEs in that process. But the truth is that the procurement process is difficult for start-ups to navigate; it has been for a long time. Often, they are unwilling to start on the process of understanding how to navigate a system that has been well-navigated for a long time by a handful of very large organisations. It is a challenge both ways. We need to change the culture on the start- up side , but government has to be more open-minded to it as well.

If you look at NASA’s procurement that led to the creation of SpaceX or the first SpaceX deal in 2006, the company was barely three years old. I do not think it had anything but a business plan in front of it. That was almost 20 years ago, and SpaceX is now the leading private space company in the world — if not the leading space institution , full stop — including Governments. I do not think that if SpaceX applied today to the UK Space Agency it would be able to get through the procurement process with where it was as a company. I say that as a member of the Industrial Development Advisory Board where we see some of the applications that come into UKSA.

There is still a very stark challenge. It is increasingly important as software becomes more prevalent in almost every industry. You will see this in healthcare, transportation, agriculture, and increasingly in defence. The more that government can do here to lower the barriers to entry and to allow people to experiment , the better.

I absolutely echo James’s comments about risk appetite and the role the Government can play in procurement. Even when companies get in, we have seen examples of hitting milestones and KPIs and then the contracts being ended anyway. That is almost worse, because the signal you are sending to the private sector is that something has gone wrong here. That is the other element. Even if they manage through, there is a responsibility of continuation and following up.

Q18 Thank you. I would agree with that. Alex and Mike, please add anything on procurement, and then I am interested in your view on what the Advanced Research Invention Agency — ARIA — might do. Alex, you have already commented on Innovate UK, but how would you like it to be configured, or do you think we should get rid of it and spend the money with one of the new agencies? Do you have a view on how the Regulatory Innovation Office should best be set up?

I am not sure Wayve is in a great position to comment on government procurement, so I will pass on that question. On ARIA, I have spoken at length with Ian and Matt and others. Going back to the talent piece, the Government have done a fantastic job of getting great talent around that, so I am confident that great things will come as a result. As to what they are, I am not sure yet. I have seen some really interesting strategic questions posed about where and how to invest to make the most of AI technologies. The UK has some really big gaps in infrastructure, compute and power.

Getting the benefits of self-driving cars being on the roads everywhere throughout the UK , as an example , will require a complete overhaul in many different areas of infrastructure to be able to optimise them over time. It is early days. It has been a couple of weeks since the Regulatory Innovation Office was announced. If we had that five years ago, it would have been amazing. We were working out of a garage in Cambridge, building our start-up, and trying to knock on the door of government saying, “Hey, we’ve got this new idea of self-driving cars. Can you make it legal?” It was an impossible task. If we had had a method to navigate through that, that would have been great. Today, I have this opportunity to speak to you all and have a conversation with government. Five years ago, that was so far from the truth.
We are not government.
Sorry , to speak to the Lords.
Parliament.

Yes. I think that is a great concept. I am optimistic. I hope it helps others in our position going forward, whether they are trying to change other significant opportunities in deep technology or things like this. I feel optimistic and I hope it can shortcut a lot of the process that we had to go through to be able to see more change to support our product.
I will echo that there is generally some quite strong positivity around ARIA and what it may end up achieving, and it is generally supported by the community that I represent.

Regarding Innovate UK, there is still quite a lot of frustration with the bureaucracy involved and the time it takes, and even in some cases the outcomes and the explanation of the outcomes in accountability for where the taxpayers’ money is being deployed and for what reason. I have heard that on both the academic and the business side. I am not the expert on grant funding , but I certainly think that is an area that—
Is your sense , then , that it is about slimming down the grant application process, or is it that we need to start again with the whole premise and the concept of it?

The concept of it is very valuable in what it is there to achieve. It is highly valued as the central source of funding for many very small businesses and start-ups. I think it is the implementation and the execution. In some cases, it is clearly a bit of a black box from our side on the decision-making process and reference was made in some cases to whether the outcomes appear linked to a political objective more so than what the actual business case would be. As a principle, it is very valuable. It is really the implementation or the paperwork involved for the start-ups that has been a pain point.

I have one specific comment on the Regulatory Innovation Office , particularly where there is a new product or service and how that will be captured by regulation. Particularly from an Imperial perspective, having regulation of convergent science at the heart of the new office would be beneficial, where different disciplines are coming together to form a new proposition or product that might not be covered by existing regulation, and making sure those types of things do not fall into the cracks. That is often where there will be a new opportunity or a new innovation .

Q19 Thank you. Finally , is there anything else that you think government should be doing to help scale-up? Is there more that DSIT should be doing to support exports? This is your final chance to feed into our thinking for this inquiry.

I would love another 90 minutes to discuss that. Just taking a step back and trying to pull some of these threads together, whether it is procurement, Innovate UK or other institutions here that we have spoken about, what ARIA is doing slightly differently is that it is very proactively reaching out and looking for opportunities and seeking them. As a state, we have been incredibly reactive. We say, “We want X. Please fill in the forms and jump through the hoops, and we’ll give you the money to do it”. We need to be far more proactive in what is an increasingly volatile world, whether that is when it comes to regulation or funding—dare I say it, more of a venture mindset when it comes to seizing these opportunities—and culturally that is something that government has not yet seized. Across the board, all these institutions could benefit from thinking that way.
Thank you.

A lot of the ideas that have been posed are great. It is an injection of pace — to James’s point — scale, and harmonisation across the various initiatives. There is a risk of duplication in some of the items that we are talking about. I am really supportive of the RIO, but how do we ensure that we are not just layering regulation on regulation and stifling growth? Those would be a few things.

There is one more that just popped into my mind. While there are gaps domestically, whether it be capital talent or growth, there is an opportunity to aggressively target and bring in talent and innovation companies globally. That will foster amazing domestic growth. Other countries are doing that much more aggressively. It is not just about money; it is about narrative, openness and being welcoming, and it is something that I just wanted to put on the table.
It is a point well made. Is there any final comment before we stop?

I would love to make one comment on exporting technology, policy and products. Right now, we have developed software that can drive cars autonomously and safely, and we are trying to export this into major markets and automotive manufacturers such as those in Germany, Japan and the United States. A lot of this requires engagement with regulators in those domains. There are a couple of asks that we would love to see from government that are absent today. When we go to Germany and look to meet regulators there, having introductions from the UK Government would be a powerful way to get in. We have had to navigate our way to those introductions through commercial relationships. There is a huge opportunity for government to help navigate those.
The Department for Business and Trade does that for us in education through an education export tsar-type person, but you do not have access to that in your sector.
No, not in transport, unfortunately. We have been asking and have not seen that effectively done so far.

The second constructive ask we would love to get is this. We do a lot of international policy work. I have a fantastic policy team that sits on the UN committee to look at global autonomous driving regulation. We co-chair one of these committees with BMW. Countries like Germany and Japan will gather together industry leaders, mutually agree a position and then go with a powerful ask to these committees.

In the UK, our experience has been that we find out the UK’s position in the meeting. I would love to see a collective and unified message that can be brought together from public and private stakeholders and for us to go together to drive change. The Automated Vehicles Act in the UK is a great example of innovative regulation that is ahead of other markets. If we could bring that leading message and align other regulators to follow suit, it would be a real advantage for us to get this technology out there. I would love to see that.
That is a really powerful point.

My final comment relates to a question I did not manage to come back to about why there was some pessimism from our scale-up CEOs about what is to come. One specific point comes back to some extent to the topic of talent and more specifically employment law changes and the flexibility of the labour market. The reality is that most start-ups and scale-ups do not go through the seamless success story that Alex’s business has gone through. The reality is that many of them go through stops and starts and have to restructure, pivot and be adaptable. When you compare the US market, which is not what I am suggesting we should replicate, we can learn from the level of flexibility and therefore risk-taking of companies as they are making these decisions and pivoting their businesses, and the amount of adaptability and nimbleness that those businesses can show; and that is a point of concern noted from some of my community.
Q20 If you had a magic wand, what is the one thing you would like to see from the Budget?

Anything we can do to improve access to compute in this country and infrastructure would be a huge advantage, and trying to avoid any political hot potatoes is probably a good thing , I think we can all agree .

That segues into where I was going to conclude, which was to say, alongside a huge thank you to all four of you for your fantastic contributions today, you have been very rich with the information that you have provided. It is hugely helpful, and I am very grateful to you for the time that you have taken and for the preparation that you have clearly given to come here and give evidence to us today.

We have the Budget tomorrow, of course. Lord Knight said to Mr Wise that this is your final opportunity. If there is anything that you reflect on having given evidence to us today that you would like to follow up with any supplementary written evidence, you are more than welcome to do that. Please contact Dan or Anna, and we can draw on that too in terms of further written evidence. Indeed, if there is anything that comes out of the Budget tomorrow that you would like to refer to—because, clearly, we are doing this in advance of that—that would be hugely helpful, too. On that note, t hank you again.

sessions.iT: The Grey Belt
sessions.w: Calderdale Council; Greater Cambridge Shared Planning; Solihull Metropolitan Borough Council

segs.tx: Built E nvironment Committee
C orrected oral evidence: The grey belt
Tuesday 22 October 2024
Watch the meeting

Members present: Lord Moylan (The Chair); Lord Bailey of Paddington; Lord Faulkner of Worcester; Lord Greenhalgh; Viscount Hanworth; Baroness Janke; Lord Mair; Lord Mawson; Baroness Miller of Chilthorne Domer; Baroness Warwick of Undercliffe; (Kelvin MacDonald, Special Adviser to the Committee).
Evidence Session No. 2 Heard in Public Questions 20 - 2 8
Witnesses

I : Richard Seaman, Corporate Lead for Planning, Calderdale Council; Stephen Kelly, Joint Director of Planning and Economic Development, Greater Cambridge Shared Planning; Mark Andrews, Head of Planning, Design and Engagement Services, Solihull Metropolitan Borough Council.
Examination of witnesses
Richard Seaman, Stephen Kelly and Mark Andrews.

Q20 Welcome to this meeting of the House of Lords Built Environment Committee. This is our second evidence session in the short inquiry we are conducting into the proposals for the grey belt. My name is Daniel Moylan and I chair the committee. I will not introduce the other members of the committee at this stage, but I will call them by name when they wish to ask a question.

Today , we welcome as our witnesses and guests Richard Seaman, the corporate lead for planning at Calderdale Council; Stephen Kelly, joint director of planning and economic development at Greater Cambridge Shared Planning; and Mark Andrews, the head of planning, design and engagement services at Solihull Metropolitan Borough Council.

We are going to ask some questions. I ask you, with every respect, to seek to keep your answers reasonably crisp and to avoid repetition, in the sense that if one of your colleagues has given the answer you would give there is no need to repeat it. All the evidence is recorded and a transcription is made. It is not reinforced by being said twice, but, of course, you may want to emphasise something a colleague has said. I do not want to be overrestrictive, but repetition simply for its own sake does not add anything to the evidence base that we will consider when we come to draft our report.
Thank you very much for being here. Our first question is from Lord Bailey of Paddington.

Q21 Good morning, panel. I will start with Stephen and, if there are any additional comments, everybody else can chip in. Is the proposed g rey - b elt definition and policy clear enough for your teams to implement the policy without delay?

In some respects it is. We have undertaken a comprehensive green - belt study in Greater Cambridge. We have a clear understanding of all the land within the green belt and are able to identify and distinguish differences between low-quality land in the green belt and the higher-quality land that serves and is central to the purposes of green belt.
There are some definitional issues or qualifications to that around those who might deliberately degrade land in order to be able to diminish its purposes for the definition.

The other issue for us is around the purposes of green belt specific to a particular location. For Cambridge, the purposes are to respect the setting of the city. Matters of urbanisation and so forth that might come through grey - belt land are perhaps approached differently for places that may be reducing coalescence or keeping separation. There are matters of judgment that will become quite significant, depending on whether you are going through a local plan process, in which there is a proper means to arbitrate views, compared to, for example, the development management process, where there will be a lot of space for interpretation.

Following up the point about the development management process, there are particular issues with the two definitions. There is the definition of grey belt in the body of the NPPF and then there is the definition of land that makes a limited contribution to the purposes of the green belt. What concerns me is that the language could result in us becoming mired in legal challenges and a lot of discussions at appeals. There are certain bits of overlap across and within the definitions, such as the references to variations on previously developed land.

There are some issues with the wording. There is “not strongly perform”, “no or very little contribution”, “little contribution” and “contributes little”. All those words create a lot of potential for lawyers to argue at great length. I am very mindful that we are not just writing policy for planners like me, who live and breathe it every day ; i t has to be comprehensible to communities and to people who are making representations on local plans or planning applications. One thought I had was that some form of decision tree in the planning practice guidance might be a way to make it clearer. It worries me that a well-intentioned policy could effectively be lost in translation.
Mark, I will come to you with a slightly different question. Are there any specific aspects of the definition that you would like to see the Government reconsider?

To be honest, I would probably share some of the comments of my colleagues already on some of the definitions and the clarity that sits around it, especially th e term , “limited contribution”. The focus tends to be more towards the five purposes of green belt without necessarily considering the context of the underlying premise of green belt in openness and permanence. It will be interesting to see that worked into the consideration a little more in how grey belt relates to the overall context of green belt.
I am sorry, could you repeat your question?
Is there any particular part of the definition that you would like to see the Government reconsider? The answer could be no.

Generally, the wording around limited contribution is an area that definitely needs to be considered a little further. The idea and c oncept of further guidance to provide further definitions and information around the whole premise of grey belt is vital, as Richard set out, in providing clarity to users of the service and not just us as planners.

We have had a certain amount of written evidence that we have not yet looked at properly, although I know it has arrived. Much of it is from individual planning officers. They say that this definition will not work. Not all of them are saying that, of course, but the comments are along the lines of, “This is badly defined”. Of course, one of the purposes of consultation is to improve definitions, so it is perfectly possible that, at the end of the process, the Government would say that they have heard the comments about poor definition and have come up with a sharper and better focused definition that is clear. Would that settle your concerns, or is there a more substantive objection to the policy that you want to articulate?

My view is that what the policy is trying to achieve is laudable. The problem is that a lot of this just comes down to how it is structured, how it is presented and the choice of words. It will cause enormous uncertainty and legal dispute.
But th e definition could be refined.

Absolutely . As I mentioned, it is things like the choice of words, where you have “little contribution”, “limited contribution” or “contributes little” . T hat might , on one level seem , innocuous —

I completely understand that “ limited ” , “ little ” and so on are words that require a high amount of judgment and may open it up , but they could be removed or changed. If they were, you would have much less concern about the whole thing.
Yes.

One needs to read some of the interpretation, as Richard has highlighted, in the round. Certainly, there are elements in the definition of grey belt that perhaps do not go far enough in offering clarity. One of our comments as the local planning authority was around the potential for the release of grey - belt land in its purest form to progressively erode the green belt and the purposes of the green belt. Within the definition, there is certainly a suggestion that consideration be given to adjoining parcels of land in determining whether the release makes a limited contribution to the five green - belt purposes . O ne can envisage a circumstance in which you end up with either severance or enclosure of adjoining land that, in turn, denudes that adjoining land. The definition as it stands just stops at references to paragraph 140 of the framework. I t could do with some further clarification on potential erosion.
You would want to be able to take the physical context into account more fully.

Absolutely, particularly for releases on villages , or where you could see coalescence happening, where the release of potentially low-performing or even previously developed land would change the shape of the build pattern or the interplay between the different settlements around, such as to capture effectively quite high-quality and important green - belt land but so denude it from contributing to green - belt purposes that it undermined its own continued status.

Specifically for you, Mr Kelly, you refer to concerns about those who deliberately degrade land. Do you have any evidence that this has been happening, or are you expressing a fear that it would happen if this definition and this policy went through?

I do not have specific evidence, but one of the lessons that we have learned from, for example, biodiversity net gain and the processes around that is that the protocol and obligations had a backward look to ensure that deliberate attempts to denude the biodiversity of a particular site would not in themselves justify enhancement of biodiversity. I am conscious that a number of temporary uses that could take place on green - belt land , either under permitted development or in respect of operational works and construction works , might be seen as a foil to facilitate a subsequent change in the status of the land. Contemplating that within the NPPF might be a useful reflection for the policy authors.

Q22 My question is about opportunity and the concept of the grey belt. Would using the grey - belt definition identify new possible sites for development above and beyond those that you have already identified through the local plan process? That is open to the three of you. I would like to hear your comments.

Within Calderdale , we undertook a green - belt review to support our local plan that was adopted 18 months ago. That was a policy - off exercise. We did not carry out the green - belt review to identify housing sites but as a piece of evidence to support the housing sites.

I am mindful that, in the green belt, green - belt policy is still only one consideration with regard to land that you might release. There was land in Calderdale that we did not release that would fall under the category of grey belt. We did not release it for reasons around sustainability or flooding. We have a lot of brownfield land , mills in the Calder Valley and old industrial sites, that suffer very badly from flooding.

Conversely, we released what you might call high-performing green belt because it met wider sustainability considerations. There is grey - belt land within the green belt in Calderdale that could come forward, but it is often constrained. There can be issues of flooding , and t here is a particular part of Calderdale where we took a decision not to release further land because of transport infrastructure. If you did a fresh green - belt review now and a fresh site assessment process, I am not sure that you would identify a lot more land. Obviously, as new infrastructure is delivered, you potentially could.
But not a great many additional opportunities for housing on the current basis.

It would be of a modest scale. In the next few years , I do not think it would bring forward major large-scale opportunities. It would maybe bring forward smaller-scale opportunities. It gives us something to think about for our pipeline of land in subsequent plan periods.

From Cambridge’s perspective , we undertook a green - belt review. Over the last 25 years , we have released 1,800-plus hectares from the green belt to deliver over 10,000 houses and about 50,000 jobs. The normal planning process is as Richard highlights. The more recent changes in the NPPF, which remo ve the requirement to review green belts , were not something that we had followed in our plan-making process, partly because , in identifying the most sustainable way of developing a locality and talking to our communities about their priorities for defining those spatial principles means , that it is important. We have about 24,000 hectares of green belt and t hat is an important part of the debate locally.

We have promoted, and are already promoting, further releases from the green belt in Greater Cambridge , both for housing and particularly for commercial development around Addenbrooke ’ s Hospital, which is an international centre for life sciences. We have already given consideration to the expansion of the definition to require us to consider grey belt. Indeed, by and large, the grey - belt locations are more dispersed locations on the edges of our villages in the green belt , and are not the most sustainable locations for further growth.

To provide a bit of context for Solihull’s position, we submitted a local plan for examination in 2021 and , very recently, after a protracted period of examination, had to withdraw that plan due to a disagreement with the inspectors over, in effect, 1,700 homes on a previously developed land site. We had to balance that with the potential impact o f having to replace those homes within the wider green belt at a time when, as a local authority, we had identified well over 500 hectares of land in our green belt, including land to facilitate the arrival of HS2 in the borough, which is the first station outside London, and mining contributions and everything else towards the wider West Midlands, through the duty to co-operate.

In that respect, our plan was based on a spatial strategy that our inspectors supported. Around 50 per cent of that land was previously developed and so, to a degree, could be considered grey belt under the current definitions that are before us. Indeed, we now have around 15 planning applications for the draft allocations within that plan. The applicants say to us that, in effect, many of those sites could be considered grey belt in principle if that was to be taken forward.

What I am trying to express is that the spatial strategy that we created as part of our local plan preparation focused first on previously developed land. It then looked into the green belt. We are two-thirds green belt as a local authority area ; t he other third is already existing urbanised area on the edge of Birmingham, primarily. Land supply is limited and restricted , and constrained in a lot of different ways. Our spatial strategy focused on brownfield and previously developed land, both in the urban area and then in the green - belt area.

One of the things we highlighted in our response to the consultation was whether , when you create a spatial strategy such as that , which is in conformity with the existing NPPF, the concept of grey belt adds anything to the wider context of where we are already. If we accept that that definition will get taken forward in a new NPPF, one of the things that will be very important—something we are certainly thinking about in restarting a new local plan—is the idea of green - belt reviews and green - belt assessments and being clear on how you use those. We would welcome national guidance on methodology for how you could utilise those, being mindful that an assessment would primarily deal with the purposes of a green - belt review and might bring in things such as flooding, ecology and so on. It is about being careful not to confuse the two terminologies in that respect.

Do we think that grey belt will deliver significantly more for us in Solihull than it does currently? I am not convinced, for the reasons I have set out in our spatial strategy, but it will be interesting to see how that definition plays through the system.

There is another thing I thought it would be helpful to highlight —a pologies if this links back a little to the previous question. I watched with interest the panel last week with the RTPI and the Town and Country Planning Association. There was a lot of talk about the principle of sustainable development and ensuring that houses are delivered in the right location. That was something that struck me. It should not be houses for the sake of houses ; i t is about having the right houses in the right location, and being mindful of how they are delivered sustainably.

Colleagues have talked about the purposes of green belt and what is important for respective areas. I think that varies depending on what your green belt is based on. For us, a primary driver is the prevention of towns merging. We have Birmingham on one side of us and w e have Coventry on the other side. In effect, Solihull provides the green belt that separates those two significant cities.
But Birmingham and Solihull are merged where they meet.
The urban form of Solihull, yes. It sits on the eastern end of Birmingham.
You can drive from one to the other without knowing.

You c ould, but 66 per cent of our borough is green belt. That area is , in effect, what is deemed the Meriden Gap. That gap sits between two of the country’s biggest cities. Maintaining and respecting the gap is quite important in preventing the merger of those two urban areas. One of the things we wrestle with in Solihull is respecting the gap. It is about making sure that it is maintained in an appropriate way while still being able to support growth in the villages that sit within it and on the edges of the respective urban areas as well. I want ed to highlight the importance of that to the borough. That relates to the point about how the purposes of green belt are set out within the definition and how they are considered as part of providing additional opportunities for housing.

Basically , what I am hearing from the three of you is that this new concept adds little opportunity to your existing processes. You have quite a lot of ways of looking at releasing the green belt , other than through introducing another class, of grey belt. Is that correct?

I think so. To repeat, I think our approach has always been a brownfield - first policy , and then looking at previously developed land opportunities that might be within the green belt, and then considering the opportunities in poorer-performing parcels to deliver growth in a sustainable way.

I think context is important. All green belts are different, and they probably co - exist differently. Certainly in Cambridge, for example, we have taken an active decision to jump the green belt with new settlements. A number of the grey - belt sites, or indicative grey - belt sites , that we have explored are relatively small parcels on the edges of villages.

What we found in our last local plan process, where the plan took some time to adopt, was an opportunism that eroded the ability to focus delivery and housing development on our new settlements such as Northstowe, which you have probably heard of, and instead for landowners and the housebuilding industry to take the easy route, which is to develop small sites on the edges of villages with very low infrastructure lead times and costs. That erodes the sustainable development strategy, the public transport infrastructure and so on that we have earmarked to secure great connectivity between those new centres and new significant urban extensions.

Particularly relevant to Cambridge, Sir Oliver Letwin said that our green belt starts and stops with our local authority area. Market absorption rates and the actual number of people able to buy homes in Greater Cambridge is a rather fixed parameter . Unlike, for example, London or big metropolitan cities, where the selection of small sites that might come forward through grey belt would not impact deliverability on larger and more significant strategic locations, in Cambridge they will just scavenge from those sites in terms of the number of market purchases. In so doing, as we found in the period when we did not have a five-year land supply, that will not focus and will not locate or deliver new homes at scale on big strategic sites that are ultimately, as Richard highlighted, the most sustainable locations that we have determined with our communities for our local plans.
All three of you have increased mandatory housing targets. How is that going to affect your approach to the grey - belt policy?

Our housing target under the proposed new methodology actually comes out at a very similar number to our local plan number, which is more than the old standard methodology. Possibly unusually, we are in a fairly fortunate position.
It has increased but you have got there with your own efforts already.
We have effectively planned for the number of houses that we will need.
It is not going to have an effect on you. What about Cambridge and Solihull?

In Cambridge , the position is that we had previously identified, because of the extraordinary economic growth in the city, and significantly elevated for our new plan , a housing requirement based on the economic forecasts. In fact, the Government’s standard methodology is lower than the planning figure that we were using for the development of our joint local plan.

The proposed standard methodology increases our housing requirement by around 52 per cent , which is obviously quite a significant uplift for us in what is primarily a rural area that separates Birmingham from Coventry.

As to how the approach to grey belt will help us address some of that, as I previously outlined, our spatial strategy has always been one of focusing on previously developed land as best we can and then looking at sustainable opportunities within the green belt that are poorer performing. We are at an opportune stage at the moment in our plan-making process, whereby we have already commenced work on a new plan to try to drive forward as quickly as we can and fend off the risk of speculative development and so forth. Our focus will remain one of previously developed land first and then seeing where our evidence base takes us.

In relation to Cambridge, you described developers as scavenging what would be grey - belt sites when you did not have a five-year land supply in place. Should that not act as an incentive to you to produce the five-year land supply?
It might have been the wrong word to use for developers. The process was opportunistic.
I am not concerned about the word “scavenging”. That was not what I was trying to raise.

Often, the challenges of delivering a local plan are perhaps not fully understood. They are not always within the gift of the local planning authority. That was the reason why Greater Cambridge did not have a five-year land supply. For example, matters related to infrastructure capacity, which oftentimes rest with government, or to utility capacity, which rest with the statutory providers, cannot always be resolved.

The Greater Cambridge planning authority’s local plan process took a considerable number of years, partly because of the challenges of resolving some of those large and significant infrastructure and growth-related matters. Both the authorities that I represent, South Cambridgeshire and Cambridge City, have , over the last 25 years , been committed to sound development plan activity, but in a resource-scarce and constrained context. It was certainly not lack of will from the planning authorities to secure adopted plans; indeed, the plan that we had advanced four years earlier was eventually adopted. It was that associated infrastructure and related challenges — and indeed the examination process , where quite substantial challenge was made to the local plan itself by a range of interests — resulted in the delays that precipitated the problem.
There is lots of talk here about plans, but are you actually building the houses and communities that you want to build? What is happening in practice? Richard, it would be helpful to hear from you.

We adopted our plan 18 months ago. We had a legal challenge that took 12 months to resolve , during which e verybody was not quite prepared to take the plunge. We are now in a situation where our pipeline of major housing schemes is pretty strong. We have two garden communities , the largest of which is 2,000 units. We have the first phase of housing on one of those in the development management process. We are getting very close to the point where we are going to start to deliver, but it is important not to underestimate the lead-in time and complexity , and issues around infrastructure, which c olleagues talked about. Those are just things that you have to work with, which make it massively complex.

For the last five years, we have exceeded the housing delivery test target for Greater Cambridge. We have overachieved quite significantly in the three previous years against that target. We currently have permission for over 20,000 houses and 10 million square feet of research and lab space granted in Cambridge , and are actively working with proposals. We have nine strategic-scale housing developments of over 1,000 houses in the Greater Cambridge area, all of them consented and almost all of them on site.

The challenges we face going forward with a further suite of growth proposals relate, fundamentally, to th e availability of water to be able to accelerate delivery. I touched on market absorption rates. We found that some of the housebuilders with consents on two sites have chosen not necessarily to accelerate delivery on the second site while the first site is still continuing to build through.
In relation to Calderdale, where you have a local plan, do you anticipate getting, or are you getting, applications for non-allocated sites during the plan period?

Within our numbers and housing supply, we assume about 90 windfall sites per year. Windfalls are part of our housing supply. Because we had many years without an up-to-date plan , and because Calderdale is very constrained, a lot of the easy pickings in windfalls have long since gone. The interest we are getting at the moment is very much on the allocated sites.
Q23 Before I ask my question, I put on the record that I have no interests relevant to this inquiry to declare.

Going on from the questions about local plans —you have all given some interesting answers on those — would you say that these changes on the grey belt mean that you have to substantially change your local plans and, in effect, start again with them?

Not in Calderdale’s case. Our green - belt review was not prepared with the notion of grey belt in mind because of timings, but we have a five-year housing supply. We failed the housing delivery test for a number of years, but I think things are heading in the right direction now. I do not think it puts us in a position where we would have to review the local plan at an earlier stage. I do not think it undermines the local plan at a strategic scale. It could result in individual proposals possibly coming forward in a piecemeal or speculative way that might not sit particularly comfortably with what the local plan is trying to achieve in sustainability.
Will you have battles over the definition of grey belt?
I am absolutely certain that that will happen.
Mr Kelly, do you want to say anything about Cambridge, and particularly in answer to that last point?

Our previous local plan was in 2018, so it is quite old. Based on the work that we have previously done, I do not think we would be looking to re-examine significantly the current local plan that we have been working on, because we already had regard to the quality of green belt. Indeed, in our emerging local plan, we are proposing further green - belt releases, so we feel fairly confident about that. In areas such as Cambridge , where there is significant value in edge - of - Cambridge development, we will find quite a number of planning appeals , or indeed applicants seeking to promote development on the definition of grey belt.
Their definition.
On their definition of grey belt. In fact, we are conscious that people are already preparing for that circumstance.
Is that happening in Solihull, too?

Yes. The position we have with our local plan will probably mean that we will be at an opportune stage in being able to incorporate any sorts of changes that come forward. We have a green - belt review that we went through as part of our previous plan, and I suspect that , as part of our evidence base , we will update that. Part of that update will , I am sure, take account of any change in definitions around the grey - belt context.

Like colleagues, we do not have a five-year supply at the moment, so we are currently working with our site promoters of the sites that were proposed for allocation in our previous plan o n very special circumstances cases that work within the planning applications that they have already put to us . That will, I hope , ease some of the pressure we might find on speculative development in the short to medium term. We have already received inquiries for pre-application advice around gre y- belt opportunities, and I fully expect that we will have debates with applicants, developers and landowners about what is and is not grey belt.
It will run and run, I suspect.
Lord Mair will bring us back to some of the nitty-gritty of the definitions of green belt.

Q24 The Government have proposed three requirements for grey - belt developments: specific expectations on affordable housing, infrastructure and green spaces. I want to ask all three of you about your views on the viability of those in your areas. I specifically want to ask a bit more about affordable housing. The requirement is that at least 50 per cent should be affordable housing , with “an appropriate prop ortion being social rent” , subject to viability. We have received written evidence that the viability of the 50 per cent affordable housing has been identified as a potential barrier to grey - belt development. In fact, we have received written evidence expressing scepticism about that target. Can I ask all three of you about that, starting with Calderdale?

When we prepared our local plan, we carried out a desktop viability exercise for every site allocation. The broad position in Calderdale, a former industrial area in West Yorkshire, is that brownfield land in general does not achieve benchmark land values. It is not viable without policy concessions or public subsidy. If you take relatively straightforward greenfield land in the strongest-performing market areas of Calderdale, 30 per cent affordable housing is viable. There is nowhere in Calderdale where you would deliver 50 per cent affordable housing without public subsidy.
What about in Cambridge?

Because of the higher values that exist in Cambridge, I am not sure that 50 per cent would render a development unaffordable, but it w ould be highly contingent on the other associated infrastructure costs. The expansion of the city of Cambridge is reaching a point where there are potentially significant additional infrastructure costs. What we have sought to try to do — particularly around transport and proximity to major junctions — in the context of how we fund strategic infrastructure development , and whether the additional development and the loading on it based solely on grey - belt land is likely to render sufficient receipts to be able to resolve that, I suppose poses a question. From a market perspective, I suspect that value uplift from a number of our grey - belt sites that are not largely or significantly contaminated is probably capable of delivering 50 per cent affordable.
What about in Solihull ?

Across our borough, we have quite a disparity in values ; the difference between the north of the borough and the middle and south of the borough can be quite significant. At the moment, we have a policy position of 40 per cent affordable housing . I n the first instance, an increase to 50 per cent may not seem significant, but it is coupled with a relatively high CIL charging schedule in place and related Section 106 contributions that will be required in site-specific circumstances, as well as meeting the other tests . W e have not tested what a 50 per cent affordable housing figure would do ; t hat was not part of the viability evidence that supported our plan. A lot of the anecdotal evidence we see on the viability pressures being talked about from applicants in the industry and developers we have spoken to would suggest that pushing that 40 per cent to 50 per cent could start to cause issues for us in wider infrastructure delivery.
You were going to say something, Stephen.

C an I make another point? The whole thrust of the Government’s narrative around grey belt presumes that residential is the only purpose that this grey - belt land will be put to. In Greater Cambridge, there is a very vibrant economy, and that means that residential is not the highest land value in Greater Cambridge. That falls on laboratory spaces, research institutions and so forth. In that context, there is a real skew in the golden rules from the NPPF to presume that the benefit from green - belt releases that are sought through the additionality of a grey - belt site release—the exceptional circumstances, in a sense, of the grey belt—is focused on residential development.

In Cambridge, commercial lab and research space is higher-value land than residential. It creates significant housing challenges through the population that it brings to the city. Looking at the golden rules and the proposals that are being suggested to my local planning authority for commercial lab development, it looks like a very low public benefit in addition that arises. There would be no requirement, as it is drafted, to contribute towards the delivery of affordable housing. I do not necessarily see why that could not be the case, but it relates it to housing development. Likewise, the delivery of necessary infrastructure is the same test as in any other planning application , having regard to the CIL requirements.

The delivery of green space from commercial development is, in a sense, part of the proposition these days for attracting employe e s and occupants. Distilled through the lens of commercial development, the release of grey - belt land seems remarkably generous to commercial development opportunities, and in Cambridge that is probably the favoured land release for all the pressure that our green belt will come under. We have already proposed a significant release around the biomedical campus, but further land around the perimeter of Cambridge is already being developed by commercial lab, science and digital institutions.
Richard, you were going to say something about Calderdale.

Returning to the issue of viability, we have something of a viability double whammy in the sense that we do not have high land values but delivering development in Calderdale is relatively expensive. We have high infrastructure costs. If you have visited the Pennine areas , you will know that a lot of our land is very steep , and so a lot of civil engineering is involved to make sites developable. Viability is a very big issue for us.

Would I be right in concluding from what the three of you have said that these three particular requirements— on affordable housing, infrastructure and green spaces—are actually applicable anyway to release of land on green belt , irrespective of whether it is grey belt or not? There is nothing particularly special about grey belt, is there?

I would argue that the appropriate mechanism to consider affordable housing percentages is through the local plan process, where there is an evidence base, it is supported by a strategic housing market assessment and by viability evidence, and then you set zones within your plan area , dependent on the market conditions. A one-size-fits-all 50 per cent would be very problematic in somewhere like Calderdale.
Stephen and Mark, do you want to add to that?

I was just going to echo that point. With the disparity in values that we have across the borough, I feel that an affordable housing policy set within a local planning context feels the more appropriate way to do that, based on a locally informed evidence base, community engagement and that sort of thing, as well as having regard to local housing needs around types, tenures and so on.

Perhaps a bit more widely, I have a point about those three tests. I found it quite interesting that open space is then separated into its own additional paragraph in the draft NPPF, which almost feels to be elevating it a little in the infrastructure contributions that might be provided as part of those sorts of sites. The overall wording would benefit from something that specifically focuses on local policy and local infrastructure requirements as established within a local plan, similar to affordable housing requirements.
There is the key phrase “subject to viability”, which of course has been described in a number of our written contributions as being a get-out clause. Is that fair?

You have to refer back to how viability is dealt with in the annexe, which suggests a singular approach to benchmark land values, as I understand it. The NPPF , or the practice guidance , would set the benchmark land value. If you look at green belt across our three boroughs, you find that the values will be very different. They can be different in Calderdale between two sites on opposite sides of the road. The annexe on viability need s to be looked at ; I do not think it is sufficient just to say “subject to viability”.
Stephen, do you have any more to add?

Only a comment about the ability of local housing strategies to be able to adjust and respond to this, and in that broader vein the role of things such as local nature recovery strategies and the potential for them to be unravelled by piecemeal developments that seek to deliver open space as a consequence of the golden rules in places where there is the development of biodiversity net gain —my authority is not alone in this — h abitat recreation opportunities and so forth. They are not necessarily complementary when trying to re-establish habitat and space on the edges of new settlements to promote increased public access. Those broader sustainability objectives and the golden rules may well lead to some slightly perverse outcomes in the delivery of wider green infrastructure and environmental objectives.

Q25 This is for Mark Andrews. I imagine that , in your area , there is plenty of former industrial land. How does that feature in your plans? Should your plans be affected or modified in any way in the light of the grey - belt proposals?

In that respect, may I supplement something else you could take in when you are answering Viscount Hanworth? Are there any peculiar decontamination-type issues that will arise in the grey - belt sites, or are they just the same as other brownfield sites? I raise this because there has often been reference made to redundant petrol stations and things like that, which to my mind implies a high level of decontamination requirement. Is that an issue worth considering, or is it just the same as it would be for any other previously used site? Viscount Hanworth’s question is the key, but if you would throw decontamination into the answer it would be help ful .

As a borough, we do not have a significant amount of former industrial land. We have some old mining legacy sites and things like that towards the north of the borough, and one of those at the moment is caught up with the work with HS2. It is a site called Arden Cross , towards the north of the borough , near the M42. O nce HS2 was identified as arriving in the borough, we worked jointly with HS2 and the respective landowners to develop the concept of an urban village in and around that site. That was one of the flagship schemes in our draft local plan. It is still a flagship opportunity for the borough , and is very much about creating a sustainable urban village around the arrival of HS2.

Generally speaking, as I outlined before, our overall spatial strategy is one of focusing on previously developed land wherever we can. I know from previous experience working in other urban authorities where there is a lot of disused industrial land and opportunities to redevelop it that it is about getting the balance right between releasing for housing previously developed land that was generally for employment use or retaining it for employment opportunities.
This is industrial land or ex-industrial land that is in the green belt.
Yes.
That is what is really of interest to us.

Yes. It is about getting the balance right between whether the land is most appropriate for housing or whether it is still most appropriate for commercial or employment opportunities. It is about working that up, I suppose, through a local plan.

For Solihull, it is not a significant issue. We have previously developed land within our green belt, and that has become the focal point of some of the sites we took forward in our previous plan and will undoubtedly be carried forward into our next.

To pick up you r point, Chair, about the decontamination side of things, that will potentially be an issue for grey - belt sites, especially if they are sites that had not been considered under the previous framework . I suspect that the impact of that would be broadly similar to any other case we may have coming forward through a planning application. Where there may have been former industrial use on that site, there will be a need to undertake an appropriate assessment of land contamination.

Cambridge is different from Solihull — an urban core surrounded by a circumferential green belt but punctuated on a map by white spots. I am thinking of a research establishment in the life sciences that is vying for expansion and is located in an isolated country estate with listed buildings. How does your plan accommodate such cases? I could probably put a name on what I am trying to describe—Babraham. Is that an appropriate instance?
Viscount Hanworth is a professor at the University of Cambridge.
I am not. I am not in the life sciences either. I am a mathematician at Leicester , but b e that as it may.

W e have already contemplated , through green - belt releases that we were proposing , the expansion of that particular institution and removing further land that surrounds it—it is an island within the green belt—from the green belt as part of the local plan process. The point I would make is that most progressive planning authorities are acutely conscious of the sustainable development obligations, and councillors in Greater Cambridge share and understand the need from a national priority point of view .
